description: We’re Mango’s Gravity, a team of high school engineering students from EJ KOSEN in Egypt who believe that if an apple inspired Newton, a mango can power our next space hack. Combining software, AI, hardware, web dev, and data analysis for this year's NASA Space Apps Challenge, we're convinced Ismailia is secretly the next space tunnel to deep space. When we're not crunching physics or debugging code, we’re busy building real tech and figuring out how to grow tropical fruit in the cosmos.
summary: Our Project is a Clear Map representing Mars's clear path for the Jezero Crater Mission for the first astronauts on Mars. It does not just display Mars data, it turns layered NASA data into a route an astronaut can actually walk, then tells the crew whether that walk is survivable. And we faced alot of challenges while developing this web app, like learning how to use "USGS-NASA Planetary Geologic Mapping" To build images for the unsafe places and hazard detection using Mars geologic data and implementing the JPL Mars Trek library using Leaflet.js and organising all of the work while we all faced the "MidTerm" exams. Our project implements real Mars data from NASA, telling future astronauts that it will be safe to go there, and we are making sure everything is ready for them and calculated.
details:
What this is

MarsGo is a Python web app prototype for planning a hypothetical astronaut walk—an EVA—around Jezero Crater on Mars. Instead of just displaying Mars imagery, it combines terrain, geology, rover history, suit-consumable estimates, weather and radiation assumptions to suggest a route and give a GO / NO-GO planning verdict.

Its intended impact is to make exploration data more useful for human mission planning: help a crew consider where to walk, what science to do at stops, and what hazards or resource limits matter

Github Repo: https://github.com/asaadzx/marsgo

Stack

  • Language(s): Python 3.12; Dockerfile for packaging.
  • Framework: Streamlit web app, with Folium/Leaflet maps.
  • Notable libraries: NumPy, SciPy, scikit-image, Pillow, and streamlit-folium.
  • Data and services: Cached NASA/JPL Mars Trek, Perseverance imagery and traverse data, USGS Jezero geology, Esri Astro CTX/HiRISE imagery, and an MSL/REMS weather snapshot. The app reads these cached files at runtime, so the demo can work offline.

How it fits together: The data scripts fetch NASA, USGS and imagery products and prepare local map layers. At runtime, app.py reads those files, lets the user choose a science objective, stations and suit limits, then calls routing.py to find a terrain-costed traverse and suit.py to assess the plan. The map and results show route distance and terrain, consumables, safety checks, station context and a verdict.

Benefits and creative choices: The central idea is to turn a map into a planning conversation: MarsGo combines a rover’s previously travelled corridor with a separate human walking route, science stops and suit constraints. The team also made trade-offs visible: for example, the terrain elevation source is coarse, so the app uses CTX image texture as a roughness proxy; it labels this limitation rather than presenting it as fine-resolution terrain truth. The weather data comes from Gale Crater, not Jezero, and is identified as an analogue. Suit and radiation values are explicitly planning assumptions, not mission rules.

Factors considered include terrain and hazards, walk-back reserve, oxygen, water, battery, EVA duration, radiation, dust, science objectives, rover-visited waypoints, offline operation and the tablet/glove-use context. The app’s main benefit is that it brings these considerations together and can explain why a proposed plan fails a modelled constraint—not merely draw a line on a map.

We used SI while gathering Data and working on the project plan and organising it only.
